sections.html: Gobiopterus species are tiny freshwater gobies (9 species known so far). They reach only 2-3 cm in length and are so transparent that one can see how a food item travels from the mouth to the end of the digestive tract.

These gobies feed on live and frozen food. The easiest food is Artemia nauplii, which are taken readily. Gobiopterus can also be found in brackish water, so a spoonful of sea salt can be added per 10 litres of water, which makes the Artemia live longer.

Gobiopterus chuno is a schooling fish and, in contrast to most other goby species, lives free swimming in the water column. Its behaviour is best compared with that of the cardinal tetra. The fish often hang in the water, twitching their fins, and then swim around in schools again.
The genital papillae of males and females look different, and the eggs in ripe females can be seen in the belly.
In nature, these tiny gobies reproduce all year round.

The red spot behind the swim bladder is the liver. It contains so much blood that it looks red because of the erythrocytes.

Lexicon: Gobiopterus: ancient Greek, means "goby with wings". chuno: after the vernacular name of the species in Bengal.
